prize_parts.citation: for showing, through a framework of skill and task demand and credible local-labour-market evidence, how technology and trade exposure reshape labour demand, wage inequality and adjustment

statement.case_for: My laureate set and my first choice are unchanged. I have tightened the citation and can now state the discovery in one sentence, as the chair asked: changes in the relative demand for skills and tasks, driven by technology and by trade, determine who gains and loses in wages and local employment, and adjustment is slow, uneven and persistent. This sentence is why I keep Katz. The skill-demand-and-supply account of the wage structure, with the Autor-Katz task and polarisation work built on it, is the conceptual half. The local-labour-market exposure designs of Autor and Hanson, with Dorn, are the empirical half. Without Katz the technology side of the discovery rests on Autor alone. I read the strands as one achievement because they answer the same question about the same object, the changing demand for labour. As an economic historian I find the persistence result the most durable finding: the historical record on railways and electrification also shows concentrated, long-lasting local adjustment costs. The work is two to three decades old and has been replicated, qualified and contested without being overturned. I treat that as evidence of maturity. I do not treat the number of members who ranked it as evidence of merit.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still attribution. Dorn is a full co-author of the central import-shock papers and is left out of my trio. Even for the strand I credit through Katz, the task framework owes much to Levy, Murnane and Acemoglu, who are not in the set, so the citation must not claim to have originated it. The Katz strand is adjacent to Goldin's 2023 prize, and the whole topic is near the 2024 prize. I judge the overlap thematic and not substantive, but I cannot verify what those citations covered beyond what colleagues state. If the Committee decides the two strands are separate discoveries, my configuration is a composite and Autor, Dorn and Hanson is the cleaner trio. The size and persistence of the China shock, and the robustness of shift-share designs, remain debated.

responses.point: Hassler moved from B004 to B037 with Autor, Dorn and Hanson. He prefers Dorn because Katz's skill-premium work sits near ground recognised in 2023 and 2024. He concedes that this leaves out the long-run education-versus-technology framing, and he credits the task strand through Autor.
responses.response: I take the overlap argument seriously, and your concession that the choice drops the education-versus-technology framing is the cost I weigh most heavily. I still differ on what the overlap shows. Goldin's 2023 prize rested on long-run evidence about women's labour-market outcomes, and the Katz strand here concerns the wage structure and the demand and supply of skills. That is adjacent ground, not the same finding. Crediting the task strand through Autor is coherent, but then the citation narrows toward the trade-shock design, which is the more contested part. I do not think my reading is clearly right. Your trio is the sensible variant if the Committee wants a prize tied to the import-shock evidence, and I would not oppose it on scientific grounds. I will also say that, as an economic historian, I may read the Goldin adjacency differently from members outside my field.

responses.point: Dreber moved to Autor, Dorn and Hanson because omitting Dorn would misstate where the import-shock evidence came from. She frames the citation around credible evidence rather than the whole skill-premium history. She weights robustness of evidence most heavily and remains attracted to B008 for a trade prize.
responses.response: I agree that Dorn's role in the import-shock papers is real, and that a citation naming only three people has to be honest about the cost. Your robustness criterion is one I share, and it is why B008 is my first alternative. Its selection and reallocation mechanisms have been checked across many countries. I part from you on scope. A citation tied only to the import-shock evidence asks the Committee to rely on the strand whose magnitudes are most disputed. It also leaves the general lesson about technology and labour demand to Autor. I keep Katz for that reason. I do not count it as decisive. I would accept either third name over a two-name award, and I would not support using Helpman twice across B004 and B008.

responses.point: Teorell reads B045 as complementary to the 2024 prize. The 2024 prize asked whether colonial institutions explain long-run prosperity, and B045 asks how specific rules shape fiscal and policy choices. He regards B037 as scientifically very strong but composite, with a Katz-versus-Dorn cost.
responses.response: Your distinction moves me. In round 1 I was unsure that B045 was separate from the 2024 prize. A question about the long-run origins of prosperity differs from a question about how electoral and constitutional rules shape fiscal outcomes within a polity. That makes me less worried about adjacency, and I defer to you on how distinct the field is. My remaining concern is identification in the cross-country constitutional evidence. What would reduce it is evidence that the predictions about electoral rules and fiscal outcomes have held up in designs with credible variation, and that the credit for Besley's strand can be separated from Persson and Tabellini's. I agree that Persson and Tabellini alone is the natural fallback. Your composite point about B037 is fair and is my own main reservation. It is the reason B045 stays an alternative and I do not place it second to nothing. I still judge B037 the broader advance, and the shared object, labour demand under technological and trade change, is what keeps it one achievement for me.

responses.point: Friberg answered my round-1 question about method versus discovery. He argues that BLP changed which quantities (elasticities, markups, merger effects) can be measured credibly, and that it is used in antitrust and regulatory decisions. He says the case weakens if the Committee wants a prize tied to a specific empirical finding.
responses.response: That answer shifts my view of B022. I called it a method, and you show that it changed what can be measured and what regulators can rely on. That counts as influence beyond a technical refinement. I still ranked it sixth because the Committee has to choose between a methodological advance and a body of findings on a general question, and B037 offers both a framework and replicated findings. B022's attribution is also less clean, with Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin outside the cap, as you acknowledge. I would rank B022 higher than I did in round 1, but not above B037. I do not hold that against it as a method.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee treats the skill-and-task strand and the import-shock strand as one discovery or two. This decides between my trio and Autor, Dorn and Hanson.
Whether the overlap of Katz's strand with Goldin's 2023 prize is only thematic, as I judge, or substantive. I rely on colleagues' descriptions and have not verified the prize citations.
The magnitude and persistence of the China-shock effects and the robustness of shift-share designs.
How far the 2022, 2023 and 2024 prizes should count against an otherwise strong case. I do not think the answer is clear.
My assessments rest on my own recollection of the literature, and I have not independently verified sources.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for B037 or the alternatives. I have no co-authorship or institutional tie to Autor, Hanson, Katz or Dorn. My research on technology adoption and labour (electrification, railways) is thematically adjacent to B037. I also work in economic history, the field of the 2023 laureate, which may colour my reading of the Goldin overlap. I have collegial ties at Lund to Andersson, and Teorell was formerly at Lund. Both are ties between members, not to any candidate. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
